definition: Rehabilitate means to bring a person or thing back to health, working condition, normal life, or a good reputation, especially after illness, injury, addiction, imprisonment, or disrepair.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word rehabilitate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know rehabilitate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Staff at the wildlife center worked for months to rehabilitate the injured hawk before releasing it back into the wild.
Mend is weaker than rehabilitate; you can mend a small tear in an afternoon, but rehabilitating something takes sustained effort to bring it back to full health.
Remake is stronger than rehabilitate; rehabilitating restores what was there before, while remaking tears everything down and builds something entirely new in its place.

Restore means to bring something back to its original condition — furniture, faded photographs, historic houses. It centers on how the thing looked or was. Rehabilitate centers on function and health: rehabilitating a patient, an offender, or a wetland returns it to working order, not to an original appearance.

Recondition means to repair something mechanical so it works well again — engines and appliances get reconditioned. Rehabilitate is for living things and lives: patients, injured knees, former inmates, damaged habitats. You recondition what runs; you rehabilitate what lives, heals, and rejoins.

Reintegrate means to bring someone back into a community after time away — one step, the social one. Rehabilitate names the whole restoration: rebuilding health, skills, standing, or working condition after illness, injury, imprisonment, or disrepair. Reintegration is often the last stage of rehabilitating someone.

Mill Creek had been written off for decades: straightened into a concrete chute in the 1950s, it ran gray and lifeless through the middle of town.
The rehabilitation crews did not try to make it pretty.
They tore out the concrete, re-bent the channel into its old curves, and planted the banks with willow.
The measure of success was blunt: could the creek do a creek's work again?
Three springs later, the answer arrived on its own -- mayflies first, then minnows, then a heron that stood in the shallows all of June.
A creek that had been a drain was back on duty, filtering runoff and holding its banks, rehabilitated in the only sense the crews cared about: it worked.
